items.item: A supplier handing over three incompatible JSON shapes isn't a data problem waiting for more storage — it's an integration cost someone has to carry, once per supplier, forever, until a shape is agreed on.

at.step: Hook: a shared shape says nothing about a value's truth

items.item: The honest prediction isn't that a standard fixes data quality — it's that structure and meaning are a completely separate problem from whether a number is true, and solving one buys nothing toward the other.

at.step: Predict: what does a shared shape actually buy?

items.item: Describing a machine model's own specification once, in a type shell, instead of copying it into every instance, is the same move as separating a dimension from its facts — just applied to an asset instead of a database row.

at.step: Reveal: one type shell, two distinct instance shells

items.item: A semantic ID is a small piece of infrastructure doing a large job: it lets two companies that have never agreed on a naming convention still agree, silently, on what a property means.

at.step: Reveal: a semantic ID outlasts whatever a supplier calls it

items.item: Choosing between an API and a file isn't a technical detail buried in an integration spec — it's the difference between data that has to stay reachable and data that travels with whoever receives it.

at.step: Reveal: a REST read and a packaged file agree exactly

items.item: A validation gate that rejects a missing semantic ID is doing exactly what it was built for; expecting it to also catch a wrong number is asking a grammar checker to fact-check the sentence.

at.step: Reveal: validation catches a structurally broken submodel

items.item: The moment a submodel passes validation, it earns a kind of trust it hasn't actually earned yet — structural trust gets mistaken for factual trust constantly, and that mistake is exactly where this topic's hook lives.

at.step: Reveal: validation never checks a value's truth

items.item: Every piece of this topic reduces to the same move: a shared shape makes data exchangeable between strangers, and exchangeable has never once meant correct.

at.step: Recap

items.item: A carbon-footprint number that passed every structural check a pipeline could run on it is still, at that point, nothing more than an unverified claim wearing a very tidy format.

at.step: Prove it: does the gate catch a wrong carbon-footprint number?

items.item: Landing a supplier's submodels in a lakehouse with a contract isn't bureaucracy layered on top of the data engineering — the contract is the only place the obligation to actually check a value can be written down at all.

at.step: Recap

items.item: This chapter closes exactly where it should: a hierarchy gave every reading a place, a historian and a gateway gave it a path, and the AAS gives the asset itself a shape everyone outside the plant can finally read.

at.step: Recap
